facts.fact: The World Bank's ID4D diagnostic, authored May 2017, states that birth registration is still manual and paper-based, that management of the civil registry relies on paper-based decentralised processes, and that the law recognises only paper registers as legal documents, a revision of the Code des personnes et de la famille to admit a digital register being in draft.

The diagnostic's questionnaire, from fieldwork of 26 April to 4 May 2016, records ICT in civil registration processes as 'planned', not introduced even partially, and the civil register as kept on paper in two books with no digital records.

The World Bank diagnostic (authored May 2017) states that no centralised digital civil register exists and that the two digital birth-registration projects are both in pilot, against 350 primary and 987 secondary civil registration centres (its source: PNDES 2016-2020).

The World Bank diagnostic (authored May 2017) states that SIGEC, begun in 2012 to build a central civil register database and connect every primary and secondary centre, is still in its pilot phase in the districts of Falagountou, Nobéré and Dissin and has not gone beyond preliminary steps; its mobile birth-registration application EDEN has not been deployed.

The World Bank diagnostic (authored May 2017) states that SIGEC was launched by the civil registry directorate DGMEC of the Ministry of Territorial Administration and Decentralization, with six IT staff deployed in collaboration with the ICT agency ANPTIC.

The World Bank diagnostic (authored May 2017) states that the objectives of the SIGEC project and of the National Strategy for Civil Registration (May 2012) include digitising the whole civil register and an SMS-based birth registration system, and that the ministry's ICT capacity does not fit them.
The World Bank diagnostic (authored May 2017) states that EDEN, the mobile birth-registration component added to SIGEC, was funded by UNICEF; it states no funding source for the rest of SIGEC.

The World Bank diagnostic (authored May 2017) states that iCivil's bubble-tag birth-registration project is ending its pilot phase with the city of Ouagadougou, with nationwide deployment costed at US$4.5 million and not yet approved at national level.

The World Bank diagnostic (authored May 2017) describes iCivil as a private initiative led by a local company of that name, partnered with the French firm Prooftag, which is pushing the government to adopt its solution.

note: Passages only. Present-tense findings are dated to the report's authorship (May 2017), questionnaire answers to the fieldwork (26 April to 4 May 2016). Health centres deliver birth notifications on paper and serve as unofficial secondary centres; no notification system is named. The document states there is no interconnection between the civil register and the identity database.
